extracted.intended_audience: scientifically literate general public; naturalists, anthropologists, and physiologists of the late 19th century
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-science research article proposing and arguing a hypothesis that human skin color and skin-structure are adaptive to different climatic types; discusses physiological mechanisms, geographic and meteorological evidence, and implications for ethnology. Focus is on relating skin features (pigment, epidermis thickness, perspiration) to five climate classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate classification (I–V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Climates are to be classified for the purposes of the argument as: I. Arctic; II. Temperate humid; III. Temperate dry; IV. Tropical humid; V. Tropical dry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each class is described in terms of temperature range, humidity, seasonal dryness, prevailing winds/breezes, and vegetation (e.g., humid temperate = moisture-laden air, limited thermometer range, breezes from warm seas; tropical humid = no dry season, dense forests; tropical dry = well-marked dry season or rainless). Use this fivefold classification when reasoning about selective pressures on skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin features best suited to Arctic climates
rubrics_metrics.description: In Arctic climates a thick integument (thick outer skin) and a light but not absent pigment are desirable: 'a thick integument is desirable... the coloring matter... will be light; but, owing to the thickness of the cuticle, the general effect will be yellow.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: frozen air increases transudation and heat loss; thick cuticle lessens evaporation; oblique sun means dark pigment would be a disadvantage. Note the need for some pigment (albinos cannot expose themselves to sunlight comfortably). Use thickness + light pigment to evaluate Arctic adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin features best suited to Temperate humid climates
rubrics_metrics.description: In humid temperate climates a thin epidermis combined with a light pigment is desirable, producing a fair complexion: 'The combination of a thin epidermis with a light pigment will give a fair complexion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: moisture-laden air reduces solar intensity (making dark pigment a disadvantage) and tends to check perspiration, so a thin epidermis promotes perspiration. Use humidity and limited temperature range as criteria to infer selection for thin epidermis and light pigment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin features best suited to Temperate dry climates
rubrics_metrics.description: In dry temperate climates a darker pigment than in humid temperate regions and a thick cuticle are required; result: various shades of yellow and brown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: larger daily temperature ranges, hotter summers and colder winters, brighter sun require more pigmentation for protection; dry air increases evaporative loss so thicker cuticle prevents excessive fluid loss. Evaluate climate dryness and temperature range to predict thicker epidermis and darker pigment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin features best suited to Tropical humid climates
rubrics_metrics.description: In humid tropical climates a comparatively lighter complexion and a thin epidermis are expected: 'the natives of such countries will be distinguished by comparatively fair complexions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: although the sun is vertical, vapor in the atmosphere diminishes its power, requiring less pigment; thin epidermis promotes perspiration where vapor tends to check it. Use presence/absence of dry season and forest cover to classify tropical humid and predict lighter complexions (e.g., Amazon valley natives lighter than Andean populations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skin features best suited to Tropical dry climates
rubrics_metrics.description: In rainless or seasonally dry tropical climates the blackest and densest pigment and the thickest scarf-skin are needed: 'the blackest and densest pigment and the thickest scarf-skin will be needed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: vertical sun at full power and strong radiation losses at long tropical nights demand maximal protection and a thick outer skin to reduce heat loss at night and guard against intense daytime radiation. Use length and severity of dry season and high mean summer temperature as predictive criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multifactorial determinants of skin hue
rubrics_metrics.description: The hue of the skin 'does not depend on [epidermic pigment] alone, but is a compound effect, resulting from the white of the dermis, the red of the blood... the color and quantity of the pigment, and the thickness of the cuticle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing causes of complexion, consider pigment amount and color, dermal whiteness, blood supply near surface (blushing/pallor), and cuticle thickness; thick cuticle amplifies pigment's visual effect, thin cuticle increases influence of blood supply (explains blushing in whites).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective function of epidermal and ocular pigment
rubrics_metrics.description: Pigments of epidermis and iris 'serve a very important purpose: they protect the tender underlying parts from the injurious effects of too much heat and light.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use protective function as an explanatory criterion: presence/absence and degree of pigment should be evaluated in light of exposure to heat/light; albinos' behaviour (avoid sun) is cited as supporting evidence. Consider reflectivity: deeper pigment reflects more rays and is more protective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspiration mechanisms and relation to skin structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Perspiration occurs by (1) secretion from sudoriparous glands and (2) continual transudation through the epidermis; 'the thicker or the more oily the scarf-skin, the less will the amount of this transudation be.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how epidermis thickness and oiliness affect evaporative cooling: thick/oily epidermis reduces transudation and effective cooling; thin/non-oily increases transudation. This links skin structure to thermoregulation and to climatic suitability (e.g., dark races with thicker epidermis perspire less).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of pigment on excitation of sweat glands
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is obvious that, the blacker the pigment, the less light and heat will be transmitted to excite these glands into activity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider pigment's optical filtering when predicting sweat gland excitation: darker pigment reflects/absorbs more incident radiation, reducing heat transmission to deeper skin and lowering gland activation; use this when connecting pigmentation to observed perspiration differences across races/climates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of atmospheric humidity in selecting for fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Humidity tends to lighten the hue (author agrees with Schomburgk and d'Orbigny): vapor-clogged air reduces solar intensity and limits perspiration, favoring thin epidermis and light pigment and thus fair complexions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess humidity (not merely annual rainfall) and its meteorological correlates (limited diurnal/seasonal temperature range, presence of haze/mist/cloud) as central variables: humid regions with moisture-laden air (e.g., Baltic coasts, Amazon valley) should be associated with fairer complexions under this theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing acclimatization from heritable adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct cutaneous changes in individuals exposed to new climates (acclimatization) are commonly observed, but 'there is no proof that these cutaneous changes are inherited.' True evolutionary change requires selection: if a skin type confers better survival and reproduction, natural selection can drive heritable change over generations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims of climate causing racial color changes, separate short-term individual acclimation (tawny/bronzed skin in Europeans in Egypt, etc.) from long-term heritable adaptation; require evidence of selective differential survival and heredity to claim evolutionary change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple lines of empirical evidence to test the theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory is to be tested against distributions of complexions at similar latitudes, observations of mountaineer vs lowlander differences, meteorological data (ranges of thermometer, length of dry seasons), physiologic measurements (thickness of dermis/epidermis, perspiration volumes), and traveler's ethnographic testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable support must reconcile apparent counterexamples (e.g., fair Englishman and yellow Mongol at same latitude) by invoking local humidity, elevation, temperature range, or other climatic factors. Use quantitative meteorological and anatomical measurements where possible; anecdotal traveller reports are used as corroborative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of single-factor dietary or disease-only explanations without broader fit
rubrics_metrics.description: The author criticizes single explanations (e.g., Foissac's vegetable-diet carbon overload; Darwin/Quatrefages' disease-selection hypothesis) as insufficient because they fail to account for varied empirical patterns; 'no reason has been shown for thinking that it is to the complexion and not to some other racial peculiarity that the relative immunity... is due.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that any proposed causal explanation account for observed geographic and physiologic variation (e.g., nomads vs peasants, Buddhists vs neighbours). Prefer explanations that address multiple lines of evidence (climate, skin structure, perspiration) rather than single-cause claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnological classification principle: color is not definitive of origin
rubrics_metrics.description: 'On this hypothesis agreement in color does not prove, and disagreement does not disprove, community of origin.' Linguistic affinities are more reliable; ethnologists should not base classification solely on color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying peoples, prioritize linguistic and cultural data over skin color; use physical traits cautiously because climate-driven convergence/divergence of complexion can mislead about ancestry. The article cites Indo-European family including fair Teutons and dark Hindoos as example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive demographic/selection considerations for future complexion change
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors moderating climatic selection include immigration and intensity of struggle for existence: e.g., in North America influx of Old World immigrants and mild selection pressure (until 'the West is filled up') delay adaptation; yet unmixed descendants show darkening of complexion over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In predicting future shifts in population complexions, consider gene flow (immigration), selection intensity (competition/harshness of environment), and generations elapsed. Use observed local populations (Ontario Loyalists, French Canadians) as case studies demonstrating partial effects.
